brief: Community newsletter for a running club: Saturday long run moves to 7am; 8 new members; club's half-marathon team finished with 4 PRs.
original_draft:
Happy Friday, runners! A few quick updates from the club this week.

First, a schedule change: starting this weekend, the Saturday long run moves to 7am. With the summer heat rolling in, an earlier start means cooler miles and more of your Saturday back. Same meeting spot as always — just set that alarm a little earlier and bring your water bottle.

Second, a warm welcome to the 8 new members who joined us this month! If you spot a new face at a group run, say hello and introduce yourself. We were all the new person once, and a friendly welcome goes a long way.

Finally, huge congratulations to our half-marathon team, who crossed the finish line with 4 PRs between them! Months of consistent training paid off in a big way, and we couldn't be prouder of everyone who raced.

That's all for this week. See you on the roads — 7am sharp!

brief: Founder letter announcing pricing change: Pro plan going from $29 to $39 in March; existing users grandfathered 12 months; adds SSO to Pro.
facts: Pro plan price going from $29 to $39
SSO added to the Pro plan
original_draft:
Hi everyone,

I want to share an important update about our pricing — and be fully transparent about why we're making it.

Starting in March, the Pro plan will go from $29 to $39 per month. This wasn't a decision we made lightly. Over the past two years, we've dramatically expanded what Pro includes, and the new price reflects the product Pro has become — including SSO, which we're adding to the Pro plan as part of this change. It's been one of your most frequent requests, and we're thrilled to finally deliver it.

Here's the part that matters most: if you're an existing user, you're grandfathered at your current price for 12 months. Nothing changes for you until then, and we'll remind you well before it does.

Thank you for building alongside us. This change lets us keep investing in the product you rely on — and honestly, we're just getting started.

— [Founder Name]

brief: Abstract for a paper on automated code-review: tool "ReviewBot" evaluated on 1,200 PRs across 8 repos; caught 34% more defects than baseline linters; 12% false-positive rate.
facts: Caught 34% more defects than baseline linters
original_draft: Automated code review has the potential to reduce defect rates and reviewer workload, yet existing tools remain limited in scope and precision. In this paper, we present ReviewBot, an automated code-review system that combines static analysis with learned models to surface defects directly within the pull-request workflow. We evaluate ReviewBot on 1,200 pull requests drawn from 8 repositories spanning multiple languages and project sizes. Our results show that ReviewBot caught 34% more defects than baseline linters, while maintaining a 12% false-positive rate that developers in our study characterized as acceptable for day-to-day use. We further analyze the categories of defects where ReviewBot provides the greatest lift, finding particular strength in cross-file inconsistencies and API-misuse patterns that traditional linters routinely miss. Finally, we discuss practical considerations for deploying automated review at scale, including reviewer trust, alert fatigue, and integration with existing continuous-integration pipelines. Our findings suggest that automated code review can meaningfully augment — though not replace — human reviewers. We outline directions for future work, including adaptive precision thresholds and repository-specific tuning, and we release our evaluation framework to support reproducibility and further research in this area.

brief: Executive summary of a data-governance whitepaper: survey of 156 enterprises; 44% have no data-classification policy; recommends 5-step maturity model.
original_draft:
Data has become every enterprise's most valuable asset — and, increasingly, its most significant liability. To understand how organizations are managing this tension, we surveyed 156 enterprises across industries and regions about their data-governance practices, challenges, and priorities.

The findings reveal a substantial maturity gap. Most notably, 44% of surveyed enterprises have no data-classification policy in place, leaving them unable to consistently identify which data is sensitive, regulated, or business-critical. Without classification as a foundation, downstream controls — access management, retention, encryption, and incident response — rest on guesswork rather than policy.

The consequences are not hypothetical. Organizations lacking foundational governance report longer audit cycles, higher breach-response costs, and mounting friction as AI initiatives demand well-understood, well-labeled data.

To close the gap, this whitepaper recommends a practical 5-step maturity model that guides organizations from initial data discovery through classification, ownership, policy enforcement, and continuous monitoring. Each step includes concrete milestones and self-assessment criteria to help teams benchmark progress.

Data governance is no longer a back-office concern — it is a prerequisite for compliance, security, and AI readiness. The organizations that act now will be positioned to move faster, and more safely, than those that wait.

brief: LinkedIn-article-length piece (200 words) on AI in legal ops: contract review time down 60% at pilot firms; caution about hallucinated citations; mentions ABA guidance.
facts: Contract review time down 60% at pilot firms
original_draft:
AI is quietly transforming legal operations — and the numbers are getting hard to ignore.

At pilot firms deploying AI-assisted contract review, review time is down 60%. Work that once consumed days of associate attention now takes hours, freeing legal teams to focus on negotiation strategy and higher-value counsel. For legal ops leaders under pressure to do more with less, that kind of efficiency isn't a nice-to-have; it's a mandate.

But the story comes with an important caveat: hallucinated citations. AI tools can generate authorities that look entirely plausible and simply do not exist — and courts have shown little patience with filings that include them. Every AI-assisted output still needs qualified human review. No exceptions.

The profession's guardrails are taking shape, too. The ABA has issued guidance on lawyers' use of generative AI, emphasizing competence, confidentiality, and supervision. The message is clear: adopt the technology, but own the output.

The takeaway for legal teams? Start with high-volume, lower-risk workflows like contract review. Measure everything. Keep humans firmly in the loop. The firms that pair AI's speed with lawyers' judgment won't just cut costs — they'll redefine what legal service looks like.

What's your team's experience with AI in legal ops? I'd love to hear it in the comments.

brief: Thread: opener + 5 tweets of cold-email tips; key stats: 4-line emails, one CTA, 8% reply rate achieved; each tweet under 280 chars.
original_draft:
Cold email isn't dead — most people are just doing it wrong.

Last year I sent thousands of cold emails and hit an 8% reply rate.

Here are the 5 lessons that changed everything: 🧵

1/ Keep it to 4 lines. Seriously. Your prospect is scanning on their phone between meetings. Four lines is enough to say who you are, why you're relevant, and what you want. Anything longer gets archived.

2/ One CTA. Not two. Not three. One. Every additional ask cuts your response rate. "Worth a 15-min chat?" beats a menu of options every single time.

3/ Personalize the first line — but make it real. "Loved your post on X" only works if you actually read it. One genuine sentence beats five templated ones.

4/ Follow up. Most replies come from the 2nd or 3rd email, not the 1st. A polite bump is not annoying — it's how deals actually happen. Silence is not a no.

5/ Track everything: subject lines, send times, CTAs. I only hit an 8% reply rate after treating cold email like a system, not a lottery. Iterate weekly. That's the whole secret. If this helped, a repost on the first tweet goes a long way 🙏

brief: Thread: opener + 4 tweets on bootstrapping to $10k MRR in 19 months; started as a $49 one-time product; pivoted to subscriptions month 7.
original_draft:
19 months ago, I launched a $49 one-time product.

This week, we crossed $10k MRR. No funding, no team, no audience.

Here's the bootstrapped playbook, in 4 tweets: 🧵

1/ Start ugly. The first version was a $49 one-time purchase — no subscriptions, no dashboard, barely a landing page. It made a handful of sales, but more importantly, it proved people would pay. Validation first, polish later.

2/ Listen for the pivot. Customers kept coming back with the same recurring problem — and a one-time product couldn't serve it. In month 7, we pivoted to subscriptions. Revenue dipped for a few weeks. Then it compounded.

3/ Do things that don't scale. I onboarded every early customer personally, answered every support email, and asked every churned user why they left. Those conversations wrote our roadmap for us.

4/ Patience is the moat. 19 months to $10k MRR isn't a rocket ship — and that's the point. Slow, compounding, profitable growth beats hype every time. If you're bootstrapping right now: keep going. It adds up.

brief: Thread: opener + 4 tweets summarizing a paper finding LLM judges agree with humans 81% of the time but drop to 64% on creative tasks.
facts: LLM judges agree with humans 81% of the time
Agreement drops to 64% on creative tasks
original_draft:
Can LLMs judge other LLMs?

A new paper puts "LLM-as-judge" to the test — and the results are a wake-up call for anyone using AI to evaluate AI.

The key findings, in 4 tweets: 🧵

1/ The headline: LLM judges agree with human evaluators 81% of the time overall. That's genuinely impressive — for many routine evaluation tasks, an LLM judge is a reasonable stand-in for a human rater.

2/ But here's the catch: on creative tasks, agreement drops to 64%. When there's no objectively "correct" answer — style, originality, taste — LLM judges and humans part ways dramatically.

3/ Why the gap? One likely culprit: judges reward surface features like structure, fluency, and length over genuine creativity. In other words, LLM judges like writing that looks good more than writing that is good.

4/ Takeaway: LLM-as-judge is a powerful tool, not a replacement. Use it for scale on objective tasks — but for creative work, keep humans in the loop. 81% is not 100%, and 64% is uncomfortably close to a coin flip.
